newsitem.title: CANADA: Canadian air fares rise due to fuel costs.
newsitem.headline: Canadian air fares rise due to fuel costs.

text.p: Canada's two major airlines, citing higher fuel costs, said Thursday they are increasing passenger fares within North America by up to five percent.
Air Canada said it is raising domestic and Canada-U.S. fares five percent.

Canadian Airlines International spokesman Paul Fowler said the Calgary-based carrier is increasing domestic and U.S. fares by five percent, also Thursday, except for flights within the Atlantic provinces, where the increase is two percent.
Both carriers said it would be up to their cargo divisions to determine whether fuel-related cargo rate increases are warranted, but that none were part of this announcement on passenger fares.

Fowler said Canadian's unit fuel cost - the price per litre - were up 8.9 percent in August over August 1995, up 20.4 percent in September over September 1995 and are expected to be 24.6 percent more this month than in October 1995.
If rates remain at current levels, Canadian's unit fuel costs in November will be 38.04 percent over the November 1995 average, said Fowler.

Both airlines have fuel hedging strategies. Canadian will not disclose its current hedge position. Its total fuel bill last year was C$396 million. For January through June, it paid C$229 million for fuel, up from C$206.1 million for the first half of 1995.

Air Canada said income from a 60 percent hedge - mainly against crude oil prices - partly offset higher fuel costs in the July-September quarter, but details will not be released until third quarter results are made public on Oct 30.
The Montreal-based airline says it has a significant hedge going forward for the next two quarters.
